diagnosis_explanation: Your kidneys have a serious problem. This means they cannot clean your blood well. You have diabetes. This can hurt your kidneys. You also have high blood pressure. This can hurt your kidneys too. You have a heart problem. It is called coronary artery disease. Your body is also having trouble with a past kidney transplant. This is called chronic rejection.
medication_rationale:
Prograf:
This medicine helps stop your body from rejecting the new kidney. It is an immunosuppressant medicine. You may notice it helps you feel better. You might feel a little shaky. Your doctor will check your medicine levels often. Call your doctor if you get a bad headache. Call if you feel very tired. Call if you have trouble breathing.

Metoprolol extra dose:
This medicine helps your heart beat slower. It also lowers your blood pressure. You might feel your heart beating slower. You may feel less tired. Call your doctor if you feel very dizzy. Call if you feel like you might faint. Call if your breathing is short.

Insulin extra dose:
This medicine helps lower the sugar in your blood. Your blood sugar was too high. You may feel less thirsty. You may need to use the bathroom less. You might feel more energetic. Call your doctor if your blood sugar gets too low. You may feel shaky or sweaty. You may get confused.

Thymoglobulin final dose:
This medicine helps stop your body from rejecting the new kidney. It is an immunosuppressant medicine. You may have flu-like symptoms. This can include fever and chills. You might get a rash. Call your doctor if you have trouble breathing. Call if your skin turns very red. Call if your heart beats very fast.
recovery_trajectory:
**Week 1:**
- You will feel tired and sore from your surgery.
- Do not take baths or go swimming for two weeks.
- You can walk short distances inside your home.
- Eat foods low in potassium.
- Avoid processed foods, nuts, and seeds.
- Call your doctor if you have a fever or chills.
- Call your doctor if you feel very sick to your stomach.
- Your goal is to rest and take short walks.

**Week 2:**
- Your pain should start to get better this week.
- You can still do light activities around the house.
- Keep avoiding baths and swimming pools for now.
- Continue eating foods low in potassium.
- Pay attention to how much urine you make.
- Call your doctor if you vomit or have diarrhea.
- Call your doctor if your urine output decreases.
- Your goal is to increase your walking time each day.

**Week 3:**
- You should have more energy this week.
- You can do more of your normal daily activities.
- You can take showers, but no baths or swimming yet.
- Keep following your low-potassium diet.
- Watch for any other new concerns you have.
- Call your doctor if you have nausea that does not stop.
- Your goal is to walk for 15 to 20 minutes daily.

**Week 4:**
- You should feel much stronger by now.
- You can resume most normal activities as you feel able.
- You may now take baths and go swimming.
- Continue with your low-potassium diet long term.
- Your goal is to get back to your regular routine slowly.
- Call your doctor if you have a fever or chills.
- Call your doctor if you have concerns about your recovery.

**When to expect improvement:**
- You will feel better over the next several weeks.
- Listen to your body and do not overdo it.
- Continue following all diet and activity rules.
- Keep your follow-up appointments with your doctor.
- Report any new or worsening symptoms right away.
escalation_guide:
CALL 911 IMMEDIATELY
These symptoms are life-threatening. Do not drive yourself.
- Fevers over 103 degrees F: This is a very bad sign.
- Severe chills that will not stop: You may have a severe infection.
- You cannot keep any fluids down: You may get too dry.
- Decreased urine output, unable to pee: Your kidneys may be failing fast.
- Signs of stroke: face drooping, arm weakness, trouble speaking. Minutes matter.
- Uncontrolled bleeding that will not stop.

GO TO THE ER TODAY
Do not wait until tomorrow. Go within a few hours.
- Fever over 101 degrees F: You may have an infection.
- Chills that are shaking badly: You may need urgent care.
- You cannot keep fluids down for 12 hours: You may get too dry.
- Vomiting more than 4 times in one day: This needs fast care.
- Confusion or disorientation, new and worse: Your body is telling you something.

CALL YOUR DOCTOR
Call during office hours. Do not go to the ER for these.
- Nausea without vomiting: This can happen while you heal.
- Decreased urine output but still peeing: Call us to check your levels.
- Other concerns about your health: We can help you figure it out.
- Questions about your medicine: Your nurse can help you plan.
